subject: Business Models
title: The Sunk Cost Trap
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Sunk Cost Trap.

hook.text: You haven't used your gym in 3 months but keep paying. 'I might go next week,' you tell yourself.

buildup.text: The sunk cost fallacy makes people continue subscriptions because they've already invested money.

discovery.text: Companies exploit this: annual plans lock you in, making monthly waste feel less painful than canceling.

twist.text: Planet Fitness's entire business model depends on members who pay but don't show up. Gyms hate active users.

climax.text: Subscription businesses thrive on inertia. The best subscriber is one who pays but never uses the product.

punchline.text: You're paying for guilt, not a gym. Inertia is the product.

quiz.question: Why does Planet Fitness prefer inactive members?

details.summary: The sunk cost trap in subscriptions is the psychological bias where subscribers continue paying because they have already invested money, time, or effort, even when the subscription no longer provides sufficient value. The accumulated investment feels wasted if they cancel.
details.whyItMatters: Sunk cost psychology is one of the strongest retention forces in subscription economics. Users who have built playlists, accumulated data, or invested in learning a platform are psychologically resistant to canceling.
takeaways: Past investment makes subscribers reluctant to cancel and lose their history
Time spent learning the product creates psychological switching costs
Companies deliberately increase sunk costs through personalization and data

faq.question: How do subscription companies leverage the sunk cost trap?
faq.answer: By helping users accumulate data, playlists, preferences, and workflows that feel irreplaceable. Every saved file in Google Drive, every curated playlist in Spotify, and every customized workflow in Notion increases the perceived cost of leaving, even if the actual switching cost is low.

faq.question: When should subscribers overcome the sunk cost trap and cancel?
faq.answer: When the ongoing monthly cost exceeds the ongoing monthly value, regardless of past investment. Past payments are gone whether you cancel or continue. The rational decision compares only future costs against future benefits, ignoring historical spending entirely.
